newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia's privatisation plan said a flop.
newsitem.headline: Serbia's privatisation plan said a flop.

text.p: Yugoslav analysts on Friday criticised Serbia's proposed privatisation programme, saying it amounted to mere window-dressing and would fail to attract foreign investment needed to revive the ruined economy.
"Privatisation is crucial for the recovery of our cash-starved economy," said Danica Popovic, of the Belgrade-based CES-Mecon centre for economic studies.
"The proposed model will not generate desperately needed fresh capital."
Serbia's Industry Minister Oskar Fodor earlier this month for the first time publicly disclosed details of a draft on "ownership transformation".
The draft obliges companies to evaluate their capital by July next year, but allows managing boards to decide whether to privatise or not.

Experts say the draft law merely preserves the existing system of vague ownership, known as "socially owned capital", without bringing about the kind of radical changes necessary to salvage the economy.
Serbia, which along with Montenegro forms rump Yugoslavia, should adopt reforms for rapid and transparent privatisation before the economy further deteriorates, analysts said.

According to some estimates, Serbia needs about $1.5 billion in working capital to kick-start idle production. Four years of war in former Yugoslavia, international sanctions and mismanagement have crippled the economy.
Serbia's ruling Socialists have been reluctant so far to join the rest of Eastern Europe in adopting a major privatisation programme.
Mihajlo Nikolic, a Yugoslav National Bank official and once chief advisor to the former central bank governor Dragoslav Avramovic, criticised the voluntary aspect of the draft law.
"Transformation of ownership is not in the interest of the present managing structure. By opting for privatisation they (managers) would jeopardise their own position," he said.
"Voluntary privatisation will only slow down the entire process and economic recovery."
The draft law would do nothing to make the government cartel which effectively runs the economy accountable, analysts said.
"Managers in those enterprises have executive power but are not responsible to anyone." said Boris Begovic, an expert from CES-Mecon economic institute.
Serbia's proposal also rejects mass or voucher privatisation which has proved successful elsewhere in central and eastern Europe.
It envisages some bonuses to employees and strictly limits the ammount of shares they could buy to only $15,000.
Government officials say the draft law does not address privatisation of big industries.
Tentative plans to sell off some parts of valuable state industries have been shrouded in secrecy and sparked speculation in local media before general elections scheduled for November 3.

Analysts say the government should conduct a public debate about how the country should proceed and adopt legislation clearly laying out the rules for small and large-scale privatisation. -- Gordana Kukic, Belgrade Newsroom, 38-111-222-4254
